title: 1 Demographic, Behavioral, & Quiz Surveys
text:
This section describes the individual-level demographic and behavioral survey datasets, as well as the specialized quiz responses. You can download the complete, de-identified longitudinal panels below.


 Download CSV Dataset (.csv)  Download R Dataset (.rds)  Download Stata Dataset (.dta)  Download SPSS Dataset (.sav)
Interactive Survey Instruments
Explore the fully digitized survey instruments for each wave below:

Wave 1: Summer 2011 Demographic Survey
Wave 2: Spring 2012 Demographic Survey
Wave 3: Summer 2012 Demographic Survey
Wave 4: Fall 2012 Demographic Survey
Wave 5: Winter 2013 Demographic Survey
Wave 6: Summer 2013 Demographic Survey

This dataset combines survey responses from 203 Notre Dame students across 6 consecutive waves, capturing demographic backgrounds, personality inventories (e.g., Big Five), academic metrics (GPAs), musical and artistic preferences, lifestyle behaviors, and campus engagement.






ImportantSecurity & Privacy Scrubbing



The raw demographic dataset originally contained sensitive participant identifiers. A secure, programmatic R script (Code/scrub_demographics.R) has been run to drop 38 personal identifying columns containing: - Participant first names and last names (firstname_*, lastname_*, v1532, v1180, etc.) - University NetIDs and emails (netid, netid_*, emailaddress_*) - Raw cellular telephone numbers (phonenumber)






Below is a quick programmatic summary of the clean demographic survey data loaded directly from the processed CSV.


Show Code
library(readr)
library(dplyr)

# Load clean demographics dataset
dem_df <- read_csv("Surveys/demographics_longitudinal_clean.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Profile metrics
profile <- tibble(
  Metric = c("Total Students (Egos)", "Total Survey Attributes", "Sensitive Columns Safely Dropped"),
  Value = c(nrow(dem_df), ncol(dem_df), 38)
)

knitr::kable(profile, caption = "Processed Demographic Survey Profile")




Table 1: Processed Demographic Survey Profile






Metric
Value




Total Students (Egos)

Total Survey Attributes
1556


Sensitive Columns Safely Dropped
38












With 1,556 attributes, variables are suffixed with a wave number (e.g. _1 for Wave 1, _6 for Wave 6) to track changes over time. Some of the core groupings include:

Demographics: Participant gender (gender_1), ethnicity, family background, and dorm locations.
Academic Performance: Semester-by-semester GPAs (e.g., firstsemgpa_2, gpa_6).
Personality Scales: Big Five traits (Extraversion, Neuroticism, Openness, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness).
Lifestyles and Habits: Alcohol use, smoking, sleep habits, and smartphone usage metrics (e.g., phoneuse*_1).
Cultural Tastes: Music genres, movies, books, and artistic preferences (e.g., bigband_1, classicrock_1, jazz_1, rap_1).





In addition to the main demographic surveys, the study administered a series of quizzes to participants. These quizzes capture high-frequency assessments of student health, emotional well-being, political discussions, and feedback on their smartphone performance.
 Download Quiz CSV (.csv)  Download Quiz Stata (.dta)






NotePII Scrubbing



The raw quiz datasets originally tracked participants using raw 10-digit phone numbers. These have been securely mapped to the standard egoid identifier and the raw phone numbers have been completely dropped to maintain anonymity.


The consolidated quiz dataset contains responses from 197 students across 146 specialized survey items, all of which are documented in the Searchable Variable Catalog.

title: NetSense Study Codebook
text:
Ego and Alter Coding Conventions
Matthew Chandler
NetSense
November 4, 2015
These are the conventions I used to code all egos and alters that appear in the NetSense data I cleaned and de-identified. These codes are consistent across the data files I have used, such that, for example, each study participant always has the same five-digit code whenever they appear in the demographic data, network survey data, or behavioral (communication events) data. Note that if a study participant appears as an alter in the behavioral or network survey data, the same consistent code is used. All other codes are similarly consistent across data files.
The codes were generated by random assignment. I used all available identifying information to match and disambiguate egos and alters across all data files.
(See the file “NetSense Data Manipulations.nb” for details.)
Three Digit

Known invalid nodes (eg, voicemail, Twitter SMS alert service)

Four Digit

Suspicious but not known invalid nodes (eg, unknown short codes, very long numbers)

Five Digit

Study participants

10000-89999: most participants
90000-99999: participants marked for exclusion because of incomplete data

(See Participant Canon for details.)

Six Digit

Non-participants
100000-199999: non-participant alters named in the network surveys
200000-899999: non-participant alters not named in the network surveys
900000-999999: reserved for exclusions, if needed

NoteSurvey Instructions



Thank you for taking this survey. Your answers will provide us with important baseline information on you and your background. The survey should take between 30-­40 minutes. Please answer all questions to the best of your ability. Some of these questions may look familiar because they were also on the 2011 CIRP Freshman survey that you took. We are asking them again because they are good questions and we need to obtain the information from you as well.
When taking the survey you can return to previous pages by clicking the “Previous” button at the bottom of a page. Please do not use your browsers “Back” button. Your answers are completely confidential. The information that you provide will only be released as summaries in which no individual’s answers can be identified. If you have any questions please email us at netsense@nd.edu. Thanks!

NoteSurvey Instructions



Thank you for taking this survey. Your answers will provide us with updated information on you and your background. The survey should take between 30-­40 minutes. Please answer all questions to the best of your ability. Many of these questions were asked during the original entry survey you took during the summer and again last winter. We are asking them again because they will provide us with information on how your opinions or situation has changed over the last semester. When taking the survey you can return to previous pages by clicking the “Previous” button at the bottom of a page. Please do not use your browsers “Back” button. Your answers are completely confidential. The information that you provide will only be released as summaries in which no individual’s answers can be identified. If you have any questions please email us at netsense@nd.edu. Thanks!

NoteSurvey Instructions



In this survey you will be asked questions about your personal contact network. We estimate that it will take around 30 minutes to complete this survey, though for some people it may take a bit longer.
This survey is very similar to surveys you have taken in the past, and its purpose is to obtain a description of how your social network has changed. This is important information that we will need to understand how social networks evolve during college.
All information that your provide to us through this survey is confidential. In all reports and presentations individuals will not be identifiable. Also, no one will see your answers except the researchers involved in the NetSense project.
When taking the survey you can return to previous pages by clicking the “Previous” button at the bottom of a page. Please do not use your browsers “Back” button.

Please answer all questions to the best of your ability. Many of these questions were asked during the original entry survey you took during the summer. We are asking them again because they will provide us with information on how your opinions or situation has changed over the last semester. When taking the survey you can return to previous pages by clicking the “Previous” button at the bottom of a page. Please do not use your browsers “Back” button. NoteSurvey Instructions



In this survey you will be asked questions about your personal contact network. We estimate that it will take around 30 minutes to complete this survey, though for some people it may take a bit longer.
This survey is very similar to surveys you have taken in the past, and its purpose is to obtain a description of how your social network has changed since then. This is important information that we will need to understand how social networks evolve during college.
All information that your provide to us through this survey is confidential. In all reports and presentations individuals will not be identifiable. Also, no one will see your answers except the researchers involved in the NetSense project.
When taking the survey you can return to previous pages by clicking the “Previous” button at the bottom of a page. Please do not use your browsers “Back” button.

title: NetSense Study Codebook
text:
On behalf of the University of Notre Dame NetSense Project team, we want to personally invite you to participate in an exciting and important research study that we will be conducting over the next two years. The purpose of this study is to learn about how social networks form and change over time and how they help to spread ideas and information from one person to another. The study is being conducted by a research team of sociologists, computer scientists and engineers affiliated with two research centers at Notre Dame, the Interdisciplinary Center for Network Science and Applications (iCeNSA) and the Wireless Institute. The research work is funded by a grant from the National Science Foundation.
You are one of two hundred (200) students selected to participate in this study because you will be a first year student at Notre Dame residing in one of the four residence halls included in this study: Pangborn, Fisher, Dillon, and Welsh Family.
If you want to participate in this study please go to our website, netsense.nd.edu, to sign up and learn more about the study. The remainder of this email contains basic information about the study and what you need to do to sign up.
If you agree to participate in this study, we will loan you a high-end smart phone, the Samsung Epic 4G, along with a plan from Sprint that includes unlimited texting, unlimited data, unlimited voice calls to and from other cellular telephones, and unlimited night and weekend calls. You will have 200 voice call minutes per month (for calls to and from landlines). This plan will be provided to you at no charge. You will be able to use this phone for your own personal use until the end of the study at the close of the academic year in May of 2013.
We will be distributing the phones to participants upon their arrival on campus between August 19th and August 22nd. At that time we will hold an orientation session during which we will provide you with information on the research project, your smart phone, and the technical support system we have put in place to help you with any problems you might have using your phone.
If you agree to participate in the study, we ask that you:

Carry the Samsung Epic smartphone with you when you would normally carry a cellular telephone
Use the phone as your primary communication device for the duration of this study
Keep the device charged and operational to the best of your ability
Return it to us at the end of the study period

The phone that you will receive will be specially programmed by us to capture in the background information that we need in order to map social networks and how they change over time. We will do this by capturing information about how you are using the phone, with whom you are communicating, and whether those communications are through voice calls, texts or emails. We will not collect information on the content of your telephone calls, emails, text messages or other forms of communication.
We want to personally assure you that great pains have been taken to ensure that all of the information gathered will be kept confidential. The researchers on this project have a great deal of experience working with confidential data and creating secure systems. We have also worked with Notre Dame’s Institutional Review Board to ensure that our research meets the high standards for security and the protection of human subject data. The details concerning what data will be gathered and how it will be protected can be found on-line on the project website at netsense.nd.edu and in the consent forms available through the website that must be signed in order for you to participate in the study.
It is important to note that all published research and reports will not include any information that could be used to identify individual participants in this study. As researchers, we are interested in general network patterns and not the specifics of any single individual’s network or usage patterns. Our research and publications will focus on network and usage patterns by looking at an aggregate of behavior (ex. male vs. female, business vs. engineering, etc.). Particularly, the research focuses on where and how different types of individuals utilize digital communications to connect to other people, not the actual content of the communication itself.
We encourage you to visit the project website (netsense.nd.edu) to learn more about our study and who we are, and to find answers to questions about the project. Please do not hesitate to contact any of the researchers in the study for further questions either by e-mail or by phone.
We hope that you will accept our invitation to participate in this exciting study. If you do decide to participate, we ask that you do the following as soon as possible:
Go to our website, netsense.nd.edu, and register for the study and answer a few questions.

Fill out the consent form.

If you are under 18 years old, download both the Parental Consent Form and the Student Assent Form.
If you are 18 years old or older, download the Student Consent Form.

Print out the forms that you have downloaded, fill them out, and sign and date them. If you are under 18 years old, be sure that your parent or guardian fills in the parental consent form and signs it.
Submit the completed and signed forms by either:

Scanning the forms and emailing the forms to netsense@nd.edu
Taking pictures of the consent forms and emailing them to netsense@nd.edu
Faxing the consent forms to Yentl Ceballo at iCeNSA: 574. 631.5952


Once we receive your documents, you will be eligible to participate in the research study. The study is limited to 200 students and participation will be prioritized on a first come first serve basis.
Please read over the consent forms carefully and feel free to contact the researchers if you have any questions or need clarification. Your decision is requested within a week of receipt of this invitation letter. Participants will be accepted until the quota of 200 students is satisfied.
Thank you very much for helping our team with this exciting and important study of social networks.
Sincerely,
David Hachen, Omar Lizardo
iCeNSA
Department of Sociology

title: NetSense Study Codebook
text:
Dear NetSense Participant,
With the end of the spring semester rapidly approaching, we wanted to provide you with an update regarding the status of the NetSense study and transition information regarding the end of the study. While we had hoped to continue the study into a third and fourth year, the uncertainty regarding federal funding of research necessitates that we wrap up the study as originally intended. Fortunately, Sprint has generously agreed to fund the project through the end of the summer. Hence, you can continue to use your phone through the first week of the fall semester at which point you will need to make arrangements for alternate cellular service as the phones will no longer continue to function. You will also be able to keep your number if you elect to use a different carrier.
You have two options if you wish to continue to use your phone over the summer.
Plan A: Turn in phone during the first week of the fall semester or earlier.

Complete a final set of three surveys at the end of the current semester. As a token of appreciation for completing all the surveys, you will receive a $5 Amazon gift card.
Arrange for an alternate cellular plan

Keep your number, transition the number into a personal Sprint account (10% ND student plan discount). The phone numbers have been pre-marked to allow for liability transition.
Keep your number, arrange for an alternate cellular plan through a different carrier (Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile, etc.). There may be fees charged by the alternate carrier for number porting.

Advise us via the netsense@nd.edu e-mail that you have transitioned the phone number
Return the phone to us by August 30th, 2013 (Friday of first week of classes). Phones can be returned to either Christine Broadbent (275 Fitzpatrick, 631-1226) or Jasmine Botello (384E Nieuwland Science Hall, 631-7095).

Particularly for those individuals studying abroad, an earlier turn-in may be desirable and can be arranged before the end of the spring semester. Shipping may be arranged as well (please see contacts above).
If you do not return our phone to us you will be charged a replacement fee of $100 for the phone. The phone will be deactivated as of August 30th, 2013 and the fee assessed shortly thereafter.
Plan B: Retain phone and purchase your own phone plan through Sprint
We have arranged with Sprint a deal whereby you get to keep your current phone. Plan B only applies if you plan to continue using your current phone. If you would like to upgrade your phone to a new phone, please see Plan A.

Complete a final set of three surveys at the end of the current semester. As a token of appreciation for completing all the surveys, you will receive a $5 Amazon gift card.
Transition the number into a personal Sprint account (10% ND student plan discount) some time before August 30th, 2013.
Advise us via the netsense@nd.edu e-mail that you have transitioned the phone number

Further Phone Subsidies
While we are not able to continue the study next year with a full subsidy of your phone plan, we would like to continue to receive data on your communication activity for the remainder of your time at Notre Dame. We are therefore offering up to one hundred current NetSense participants the opportunity to continue in the study in a limited manner. If funding allows, we may also extend an invitation to friends in your social circles with your permission.
To continue participation, you will need to have an Android phone (either your current NetSense phone or newer Android phone). Unfortunately, our agent will not function on an iPhone at this time. If you will be abroad next semester, you may resume participating when you return to ND.
The offer entails:

You agree to run a phone agent on your primary phone.
You agree to run a lightweight laptop or desktop agent on your primary computer
You agree to continue to stay Facebook friends with our NetSense “virtual” friend.

In turn, we will provide:

A monthly subsidy of $10 payable by prepaid Visa cards at the end of each semester available through spring of 2015. The subsidy will be pro-rated subject to compliance of the monitoring agents (use of device as primary phone, etc.).

No surveys or extended data collection methods will be involved. You may be asked to periodically update the agent on the phone or laptop (once per semester). Both the phone agent and laptop agent are lightweight agents that are pared down versions of our current phone and laptop agents. A new, signed consent form will be required to participate. The form will list all monitored data aspects.
To enroll in this program, please e-mail the NetSense account (netsense@nd.edu) stating your interest in participation. Please place in the subject line of your email “Phone Subsidy Program.” The subsidy option will be made available over the summer for anyone electing to exit the study before the close of the spring semester. Questions may be directed to Prof. Striegel regarding any subsidy questions.
Closing
We would like to extend our sincere thanks for your participation in the NetSense project. The data that has been collected is yielding exceptional insights into social networks and smartphone usage. Your participation has allowed us to construct a world-class dataset that is raising the stature of Notre Dame as one of the top places for research on social networks and wireless systems. We could not have done this research without you.
If you have any questions or concerns, please do not hesitate to contact any of us below.
Go Irish!
Profs. Striegel, Hachen, Lizardo, Poellabauer

NetSense Insurance / Repair Procedure – Effective 11/11/2013
With the renewal of the NetSense study, each phone enrolled in the study now has the Total Equipment Protection (TEP) plan provided by Asurion. The plan covers lost, stolen, and damaged phones (including cracked screens) and may be invoked up to twice for each line as part of the study. As the phones fall into the highest tier of Sprint devices, the deductible for invocation of insurance is $150. While we realize this is quite high, unfortunately such high deductibles are the norm for the insurance plans offered by all of the domestic cellular carriers (Asurion also services Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile).
Due to the NSF grant now having run its course and Sprint providing only service / insurance, we can no longer subsidize screen repairs nor phone replacements.
Issues with regards to manufacturing defects (ex. constant call dropping, device restarting, broken buttons) are handled separately from insurance claims and may be addressed at the Sprint store. The store will require advance notification / authorization from the NetSense study which can be requested via netsense@nd.edu. Please request authorization and we will notify you once the account has been marked to authorize you to request repairs individually.
If your phone is damaged or lost and you need to file an insurance claim, your procedure is as follows:

Please notify netsense@nd.edu immediately with the following information:

Name, Cell Phone Number, Phone Model (ex. Galaxy S4)
Your Local ND address (where you want the phone shipped)
The date of the breakage and a brief summary of how the breakage occurred
We place the insurance request through the Asurion phone insurance claim service (phoneclaim.com) with the appropriate PIN / account authorization.
A new phone is shipped to you, typically one of the order of two to three days. In the meantime, your damaged device will still continue to function.
You will provide the $150 deductible as a check (or cash) made out to the University of Notre Dame with the memo field of “NetSense insurance deductible, Ph XXX-XXX-XXXX.” The deductible may be dropped off to Christine Broadbent in the Department of Electrical Engineering in 275 Fitzpatrick Hall. You will be given an e-mail receipt denoting payment of your deductible*.
Your phone will arrive to your campus address (as provided above). Send the information on the outside of the phone box to netsense@nd.edu. Ideally, a picture of the outside box with the IMEI / MEI number would be best. Please provide a list of times that would work to roll over the service. Do not turn on your new phone until instructed.
We will do our best to port the number in the timeframe requested. Once you receive a notification from us, you may turn on your new phone.
Send your damaged phone to Asurion per the instructions contained in the replacement phone shipment. Failure to do so may leave you liable for the entire cost of the phone. All instructions are included with the shipment.
Subsequent instructions will be conveyed via text or e-mail to set up and install the NetSense agent on your phone.

* In the event of financial need, payments may be spread out over a period of time.
If you have any questions, please do not hesitate to contact us at netsense@nd.edu or to contact any of the professors in the study (Profs. Striegel, Hachen, Lizardo, Poellabauer).

title: NetSense Study Codebook
text:
Dear NetSense Participant,
We want to bring you up to date on the NetSense Project. As some of you know, the funding for the project through the National Science Foundation is now over, but we are continuing the study thanks to the generosity of Sprint. Over 100 of the original study participants have decided to continue, and we have recruited an additional 32 students. Everyone except those who are currently studying abroad should have a new smartphone. There was a delay in getting new phones for the new recruits, but most of you now have phones. Thanks to everyone for your patience in getting things up and running this semester. There are a few things we need to bring to your attention.

Surveys: As part of the requirement for being in the NetSense study we need you to complete two surveys every 3-4 months. One survey deals with basic demographic information and questions on your tastes, behaviors and attitudes. The other (network) survey, asks about the people with whom you interact.


For those continuing in the study including those who are currently studying abroad, emails with links to these surveys were sent earlier in the semester. We will be sending out another reminder soon. Please complete these surveys as soon as possible. The information you provide is critical to our research project.
For those who have just joined the study, you will receive two emails in the next few days with links to each of the surveys. Please complete the surveys as soon as you can.


Insurance: Now that we have processed several insurance claims, we have a much better handle on what the insurance policy covers and the respective costs. Attached is a document which outlines the insurance / repair procedure for your phone that are effective for any requests made on or after November 12th. The key details are as follows:



Repairs covered under manufacturer defects are the only ones that can be addressed at the store.
Any lost, stolen, or damaged phones are subject to a $150 deductible.
We realize this is quite high but unfortunately it is the standard deductible for all major US carriers as they all use the same insurance provider with similar deductibles for smartphones.
Screen repairs are subject to the same deductible. As the NSF grant is complete, we can no longer subsidize screen repairs as we had done in the past.
Payment plan arrangements may be made for those with financial need.


We strongly encourage you to purchase a case for your phone if you have not done so already.


Study Abroad Students: For those of you who are currently studying abroad and indicated that they wanted to continue to be in the NetSense study, we will send out an email in the next few weeks detailing how you can upgrade to your new phone.
Questions and Problems: If you have any questions or problems that need to be addressed you should email netsense@nd.edu. Margaret Pickard is back from studying abroad and is very knowledgable about the study and the phones. So please do not hesitate to email her if you have a problem that needs to be addressed.

The NetSense Project Team

iCeNSA Job Description: Data Analyst and Manager
This position is responsible for creating and maintaining the wide variety of relational databases used by iCeNSA faculty and researchers, and assisting iCeNSA researchers in querying, extracting, reorganizing, using and analyzing such data. Applicants for this position should have a PhD in computer science, applied mathematics or a social science discipline (with a strong emphasis on computational social science). Applicants should be very familiar with relational data sets, especially very large relational data sets, including the various types of data obtained on networks, including social networks. Applicants must have programming skills and good facility with programming languages such as C++ and Python. Applicants should also have good working knowledge of statistical software used to analyze and visualize networks such a R (Statnet/ERGM), RSiena, UCINET, and NodeXL. Because iCeNSA is an interdisciplinary research center, applicants with experience working with researchers from various disciplines within the sciences, social sciences, and engineering are preferred. This will be a full-time (40 hours per week), full-year position.

title: 1 Bluetooth Proximity Logs

 Download Academic Calendar (PDF)
Unlike the self-reported survey waves, the Bluetooth proximity data is automatically and passively logged by smartphones carried by the students. The data is divided into 34 weekly files (week8.csv through week41.csv), representing the first academic year of the study.



The smartphones were configured to run a continuous background service that scans for other nearby participants’ Bluetooth hardware beacons. When two devices detect each other within physical range (typically ~10 meters), a proximity episode is recorded.

In addition to the cleaned, aggregated Bluetooth proximity episodes, the NetSense Complete Raw Data contains continuous, passive mobile sensor telemetry streams. These datasets offer an exceptionally rich, longitudinal, multi-channel view of participant behavior across several academic semesters (2011 to 2015).
To protect participant privacy under Institutional Review Board (IRB) guidelines, these raw streams are kept in a secure, Git-ignored symbolic directory (Raw_Telemetry_Data/). Below is the technical methodology and data schema describing each of these passive telemetry channels.


Unlike the aggregated episode-level dyads, the raw Bluetooth directory contains continuous, second-by-second background scan records of the wireless environment: - Mechanics: Participant smartphones executed continuous background scans for Bluetooth beacons. It captured any nearby broadcasting Bluetooth hardware. - Raw Schema: [Scanning Ego Phone Number], [Unix Timestamp], [Friendly Device Name], [Hardware MAC Address], [RSSI Signal Strength] - Privacy Masking Note: The raw logs capture un-de-identified MAC addresses and “Friendly Device Names” (e.g., Ego’s MacBook Pro, Alter’s Laptop), which frequently contain participants’ real first and last names. In the clean files, these are programmatically scrubbed and mapped to standard numeric egoid values using the hardware crosswalk key.



Tracks the continuous exchange of text messages sent and received by participants’ devices: - Mechanics: Passenger smartphone operating systems passively recorded SMS transaction events (both inbound and outbound), logging connection endpoints and character volumes. - Raw Schema: [Sender Phone Number], [Unix Timestamp], [Receiver Phone Number], [Communication Category ID], [SMS Character Length] - Sociometric Utility: This allows researchers to model the exact temporal rhythm of text-messaging communication (burstiness, circadian patterns, response latency) and correlate text traffic with self-reported friendship closeness.



Logs voice communications, detailing phone conversations and connection attempts: - Mechanics: Records incoming, outgoing, and missed call events directly from the phone’s communication stack. - Raw Schema: [Caller Phone Number], [Unix Timestamp], [Callee Phone Number], [Call Direction/Status (Inbound/Outbound/Missed)], [Call Duration (Seconds)] - Sociometric Utility: Voice call durations represent a highly intensive dimension of social tie maintenance, capturing active verbal interactions which contrast with passive Bluetooth co-presence or short text messages.



Logs email transactions sent and received through participants’ official Notre Dame NetID email accounts: - Mechanics: Passively captures metadata headers of incoming and outgoing emails routed through the university’s mail exchange servers. - Raw Schema: [Sender ID/Phone Number], [Unix Timestamp], [Sender Email Address], [Receiver Email/Listserv Address] - Example: 5550100101, 1320120074, sender.1@nd.edu, listserv@listserv.nd.edu - Sociometric Utility: Traces academic and listserv email networks, allowing researchers to study how official, institutional communications overlay on peer-level face-to-face and text messaging networks.



Captures high-frequency geographic coordinate streams tracking physical mobility: - Mechanics: Devices logged cellular, Wi-Fi, and GPS coordinates at regular background intervals. - Raw Schema: [Participant Phone Number], [Unix Timestamp], [Latitude], [Longitude], [Altitude], [Accuracy (Meters)] - Sociometric Utility: Enables spatial density mapping, co-location clustering, and the calculation of spatial co-presence matrices (identifying dyads who spend time in the same physical locations like dormitories, dining halls, or lecture theatres).



Represents periodic backups/scrapes of the local address book directories stored on the participant devices: - Mechanics: Periodically backed up the list of saved phone contacts, capturing the active, known personal directory of each participant. - Raw Schema: [Ego Phone Number], [Unix Timestamp], [Contact Email/NetID], [Contact Name String] - Example: 5550100102, 1355893215, contact.15@nd.edu, :contact.15@nd.edu - Sociometric Utility: Maps the cognitive “potential” network of each participant—showing whom they have officially saved in their directory, which serves as a powerful baseline comparison against self-reported survey nominations and actual contact events.





For researchers seeking deeper technical specifications regarding the NetSense mobile sensing infrastructure, the following notes summarize the hardware and software calibrations documented in the primary study engineering reports:1

Classic Bluetooth Duty Cycle: The passive co-presence logs used in NetSense (2011–2014) operated under the Classic Bluetooth standard (pre-Bluetooth Low Energy v4.0). Under this protocol, smartphones continuously maintained a background scanning service while broadcasting their hardware pseudonym in a “discoverable” state. Indoor signal propagation operated in the 2.4 GHz band with a standard physical range of 10 to 50 meters.
RSSI to Distance Attenuation Limits: While Received Signal Strength Indicators (RSSI) are logged in the raw files (typically ranging from \(-30\) dBm to \(-100\) dBm), direct distance translation using classic path loss formulas is highly volatile. Multipath signal reflections off indoor structures and structural body shielding (e.g., carrying the phone in a pocket versus in-hand) create high signal variability. Thus, RSSI values in the cleaned files are treated as categorical proximity bins (identifying close co-presence vs. distal background detection) rather than precise meter-level distances.
The Episode Aggregation Window: Raw signal dropouts are common in continuous mobile scans. To prevent brief 1-second signal interruptions from falsely splitting a continuous physical encounter into multiple separate records, raw scans were processed through a greedy temporal aggregator. The aggregator greedily combined separate contact events into a single continuous proximity episode if the elapsed gap between detections was less than a determined threshold of 25 seconds.

title: 1 Bluetooth Proximity Logs
text:
In addition to the cleaned, aggregated Bluetooth proximity episodes, the NetSense Complete Raw Data contains continuous, passive mobile sensor telemetry streams. These datasets offer an exceptionally rich, longitudinal, multi-channel view of participant behavior across several academic semesters (2011 to 2015).
To protect participant privacy under Institutional Review Board (IRB) guidelines, these raw streams are kept in a secure, Git-ignored symbolic directory (Raw_Telemetry_Data/). Below is the technical methodology and data schema describing each of these passive telemetry channels.


Unlike the aggregated episode-level dyads, the raw Bluetooth directory contains continuous, second-by-second background scan records of the wireless environment: - Mechanics: Participant smartphones executed continuous background scans for Bluetooth beacons. It captured any nearby broadcasting Bluetooth hardware. - Raw Schema: [Scanning Ego Phone Number], [Unix Timestamp], [Friendly Device Name], [Hardware MAC Address], [RSSI Signal Strength] - Privacy Masking Note: The raw logs capture un-de-identified MAC addresses and “Friendly Device Names” (e.g., Ego’s MacBook Pro, Alter’s Laptop), which frequently contain participants’ real first and last names. In the clean files, these are programmatically scrubbed and mapped to standard numeric egoid values using the hardware crosswalk key.



Tracks the continuous exchange of text messages sent and received by participants’ devices: - Mechanics: Passenger smartphone operating systems passively recorded SMS transaction events (both inbound and outbound), logging connection endpoints and character volumes. - Raw Schema: [Sender Phone Number], [Unix Timestamp], [Receiver Phone Number], [Communication Category ID], [SMS Character Length] - Sociometric Utility: This allows researchers to model the exact temporal rhythm of text-messaging communication (burstiness, circadian patterns, response latency) and correlate text traffic with self-reported friendship closeness.



Logs voice communications, detailing phone conversations and connection attempts: - Mechanics: Records incoming, outgoing, and missed call events directly from the phone’s communication stack. - Raw Schema: [Caller Phone Number], [Unix Timestamp], [Callee Phone Number], [Call Direction/Status (Inbound/Outbound/Missed)], [Call Duration (Seconds)] - Sociometric Utility: Voice call durations represent a highly intensive dimension of social tie maintenance, capturing active verbal interactions which contrast with passive Bluetooth co-presence or short text messages.



Logs email transactions sent and received through participants’ official Notre Dame NetID email accounts: - Mechanics: Passively captures metadata headers of incoming and outgoing emails routed through the university’s mail exchange servers. - Raw Schema: [Sender ID/Phone Number], [Unix Timestamp], [Sender Email Address], [Receiver Email/Listserv Address] - Example: 5550100101, 1320120074, sender.1@nd.edu, listserv@listserv.nd.edu - Sociometric Utility: Traces academic and listserv email networks, allowing researchers to study how official, institutional communications overlay on peer-level face-to-face and text messaging networks.



Captures high-frequency geographic coordinate streams tracking physical mobility: - Mechanics: Devices logged cellular, Wi-Fi, and GPS coordinates at regular background intervals. - Raw Schema: [Participant Phone Number], [Unix Timestamp], [Latitude], [Longitude], [Altitude], [Accuracy (Meters)] - Sociometric Utility: Enables spatial density mapping, co-location clustering, and the calculation of spatial co-presence matrices (identifying dyads who spend time in the same physical locations like dormitories, dining halls, or lecture theatres).



Represents periodic backups/scrapes of the local address book directories stored on the participant devices: - Mechanics: Periodically backed up the list of saved phone contacts, capturing the active, known personal directory of each participant. - Raw Schema: [Ego Phone Number], [Unix Timestamp], [Contact Email/NetID], [Contact Name String] - Example: 5550100102, 1355893215, contact.15@nd.edu, :contact.15@nd.edu - Sociometric Utility: Maps the cognitive “potential” network of each participant—showing whom they have officially saved in their directory, which serves as a powerful baseline comparison against self-reported survey nominations and actual contact events.

title: 1 Bluetooth Proximity Logs
text:
For researchers seeking deeper technical specifications regarding the NetSense mobile sensing infrastructure, the following notes summarize the hardware and software calibrations documented in the primary study engineering reports:1

Classic Bluetooth Duty Cycle: The passive co-presence logs used in NetSense (2011–2014) operated under the Classic Bluetooth standard (pre-Bluetooth Low Energy v4.0). Under this protocol, smartphones continuously maintained a background scanning service while broadcasting their hardware pseudonym in a “discoverable” state. Indoor signal propagation operated in the 2.4 GHz band with a standard physical range of 10 to 50 meters.
RSSI to Distance Attenuation Limits: While Received Signal Strength Indicators (RSSI) are logged in the raw files (typically ranging from \(-30\) dBm to \(-100\) dBm), direct distance translation using classic path loss formulas is highly volatile. Multipath signal reflections off indoor structures and structural body shielding (e.g., carrying the phone in a pocket versus in-hand) create high signal variability. Thus, RSSI values in the cleaned files are treated as categorical proximity bins (identifying close co-presence vs. distal background detection) rather than precise meter-level distances.
The Episode Aggregation Window: Raw signal dropouts are common in continuous mobile scans. To prevent brief 1-second signal interruptions from falsely splitting a continuous physical encounter into multiple separate records, raw scans were processed through a greedy temporal aggregator. The aggregator greedily combined separate contact events into a single continuous proximity episode if the elapsed gap between detections was less than a determined threshold of 25 seconds.

title: 1 Social Network Surveys
text:
This section describes the dyadic social network surveys and weekly aggregated network metrics. You can download the complete datasets and survey instruments below:
 Download CSV Dataset (.csv)  Download R Dataset (.rds)  Download Stata Dataset (.dta)  Download SPSS Dataset (.sav)
Interactive Survey Instruments
Explore the fully digitized survey instruments for each wave below:

Wave 1: Summer 2011 Network Survey
Wave 2: Spring 2012 Network Survey
Wave 3: Summer 2012 Network Survey
Wave 4: Fall 2012 Network Survey
Wave 5: Winter 2013 Network Survey
Wave 6: Summer 2013 Network Survey
Weekly Aggregated Metrics: Located in Data/weekly_aggregated_metrics/ (Contains open .csv files tracking participant indegrees, outdegrees, and text/voice communication inflow and outflow across academic weeks).

The network survey asked students to nominate their peers and answer detailed questions about their relationship with each peer. These nominations represent directed ties between a nominating ego (sender) and a nominated alter (receiver).



Originally, the network surveys were scattered across 9 separate Stata .dta files (representing Wave 1 through Wave 8, including supplementary entry Wave 7.2).
A custom R consolidation script (Code/consolidate_network_surveys.R) was engineered to: 1. Parse the wave identifiers from the file names. 2. Programmatically drop sensitive identifying information (such as altername and receiver_string). 3. Strip wave-specific variable suffixes (e.g., closeness_1, closeness_75, closeness_8 are all renamed to closeness). 4. Harmonize variable types across waves to handle type conflicts safely. 5. Combine all observations into a single longitudinal panel dataset.




Below is an interactive count of dyadic ties (nominations) captured in each wave of the longitudinal panel.


Show Code
library(readr)
library(dplyr)

# Load consolidated network surveys
net_df <- read_csv("Data/network_surveys_longitudinal_clean.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Generate count table
net_df |>
  group_by(Wave = wave) |>
  summarise(
    Nominations = n(),
    Unique_Senders = n_distinct(sender),
    Unique_Receivers = n_distinct(receiver)
  ) |>
  arrange(Wave) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Tie and Participant Counts by Survey Wave")

For each nominated tie, participants provided detailed ratings across several dimensions:

Closeness (closeness): Subjective emotional closeness to the nominee (e.g., on a 1–7 Likert scale).
Tie Duration (duration): How long they have known each other in years.
Contact Frequency (freqlast3months, freqlastyear): Frequency of face-to-face and digital communication.
Emotional Profiles: Specific emotional dimensions of the friendship, such as:

emotionloving: Feeling loving/affectionate.
emotionexciting: Feeling excited/happy.
emotionsignificant: Feeling validated/significant.

Interaction Contexts (socialcontext*): Where they typically interact (e.g. socialcontextDorm, socialcontextInclass, socialcontextClubteam, socialcontextInternet).
Shared Activities (activitiesact*, sameactivities*): Activities they do together, such as studying, playing sports, partying, or talking about personal problems.





To help visualize how these social ties and emotional dimensions vary across different relationship categories, the consolidated panel was used to generate several standardized profile figures.


The figure below illustrates the proportion of emotional closeness levels reported within each relationship category. For instance, parents and significant others dominate the “Especially Close” tier, while acquaintances and coworkers represent more “Distant” or “Less than Close” ties.






Figure 1: Subjective Closeness Profiles by Relationship Type






The boxplot below shows the distribution of relationship duration in years across different categories. Naturally, family relationships (parents and siblings) exhibit the longest durations, while friendships and classmate acquaintances reflect shorter, college-coincident spans.






Figure 2: Relationship Durations Across Categories






The figure below highlights the proportion of ties that are characterized by specific positive emotions (loving, exciting, or validating) across relationship types. Strong ties (romantic partners and family members) exhibit a rich emotional profile with high rates of all three dimensions.






Figure 3: Proportions of Positive Emotions Felt in Relationships

title: NetSense Study Codebook
text:
Draft - Recommendation Letter of joining NetSense study.
Dear NetSense Participant,
With this email we are launching our initiative to recruit additional participants into the NetSense Study. Please nominate up to three of your friends to join the study. Nominated students must be currently enrolled at Notre Dame as either freshmen, sophomores or juniors. We would like you to nominate people with whom you interact a good deal. You should contact the people that you are thinking of nominating to be sure that they would be willing to join the NetSense study.
All new NetSense participants will receive the same benefits that you are receiving: a new 4G capable smartphone (the Samsung Galaxy S3 @ $100, the Samsung Galaxy S4 @ $200, or the HTC One @ $200), a free voice/data/text plan that will last through May 2015, and a good insurance plan. New invitees will also be able to port their current phone number from outside of Sprint and will not need to change their phone number (however they will be responsible for any Early Termination Fees charged by their current provider). Like with you, participants will have to purchase the phone through Sprint, but if your friends have financial need, they can request a free or subsidized phone. New participants will also have to sign a consent form, and if under 18 have their parents sign a consent form.
We are opening this up on a first come first basis. We have slots for at least 70 new participants. We will add people starting next week. You can nominate up to 3 Notre Dame or St. Mary’s students.
To nominate people you must reply to this email with the following information:

Name of each person, ranked by order of preference with 1 being the person with whom you interact with the most
Email address of each person
Gender of each person
Academic class (freshman, sophomore, junior) of each person (please note if student is enrolled at St. Mary's)

If you can, please indicate if any of your three nominees interact with each other on a regular basis.
All nominations must be received by 5 p.m. on Sunday, September 8th. We will notify the invitee of their acceptance by noon on Wednesday, September 11th.
If you have any questions please do not hesitate to respond to this email with your questions.
Thanks,
David Hachen
on behalf of the NetSense Project

title: NetSense Study Codebook
text:
Dear NetSense Participant,
Shortly we will be releasing the final set of surveys from the NetSense Project Research Team. This time there will be three (3) surveys. As before there will be a Demographic Survey and a Network Survey. You will receive emails for each of these surveys with a link through which you can access each survey.
We are asking you to complete one additional survey. As you know, we are collecting data on all the phone numbers that you communicate with through your smartphone. For many of these numbers you have told us a bit about the person associated with the number when filling out the Network Survey. But for some numbers that you frequently communicated with we have no information. For our network research it is critical that we have some information about the people with whom you communicated the most. Therefore we have compiled a list of up to 20 telephone numbers that you have communicated with a good deal. We have created a Google spreadsheet with these numbers that you can access and fill in by answering 5 simple questions about the person associated with each number. Within the next few days you will receive an email through Google with a link to the spreadsheet. Click on that link to access the spreadsheet and fill in the requested information. There are clear instructions at the top of the spreadsheet page on how to do this.
As you can imagine, this is confidential data and for that reason we have taken precautions to insure the security of the information that you will provide. Your name will not appear anywhere in this file, and the numeric name of the file is coded and only we can link it to you. Furthermore, participation in this survey is entirely voluntary. If there is a number on the list that you do not want to tell us about, please do not enter any information for that row of the spreadsheet. Also if there are any numbers you do not recognize, just leave the row blank.
We know that this is a busy time of year, so we really appreciate you taking the time in the next week to complete these three surveys. As a token of our appreciation we will email to you a $5 Amazon Gift Certificate once you have completed the two online surveys.
As always if you have any questions please do not hesitate to contact us.
The NetSense Project Team

title: 1 ARL Post-Doc Ad
text:
1 ARL Post-Doc Ad
the Interdisciplinary Center for Network Science and Applications (iCeNSA) at the University of Notre Dame will have one postdoctoral fellowship available beginning June 1, 2013 for a 12 month period. The position is supported by ARL NS-CTA project (www.ns-cta.org).
Candidates will be expected to work primarily on a collaborative project dealing the dynamic co-evolution of personal traits and social ties. The candidate will be expected to work on a novel data set containing trace logs of minute-by-minute information on the communicative interactions of a sample of 196 college Freshmen (collected via a monitoring infrastructure linked to their personal smartphones) as well as periodic survey information on their significant social contacts along with information on attitudes, beliefs and practices.
We welcome applicants from a variety of disciplinary backgrounds (e.g. sociology, political science, computer science, communication, organizational behavior, and others). Candidates who can demonstrate expertise in social network analysis or computational social science, and can provide evidence of facility with the handling and analysis of large-scale data sets will be given priority.
The postdoctoral researcher will be working with a team of sociologists and computer scientists and engineers, will be affiliated with and have office space in iCeNSA, and will be supervised by Professor Omar Lizardo. Researchers will have full access to iCeNSA’s and the Sociology Department’s collective resources in computing, print/data libraries, and administrative services.
Candidates must have completed all the requirements for the doctorate by the time of the initial appointment. Familiarity with standard network analysis platforms (UCINET, R, SIENNA) is required and facility with high-level programming languages (C++, Python, Matlab, Mathematica, etc), as well as experience with simulation and data-mining techniques is a plus.
To apply, send a vita, a short description of your current and future work, three letters of recommendation, and copies of your publications or papers to:
Prof. Omar Lizardo
Department of Sociology
810 Flanner Hall
University of Notre Dame
Notre Dame, Indiana 46556
olizardo@nd.edu

title: NetSense Study Codebook
text:
Dear NetSense Participants,
Greetings from the NetSense research team!  We hope that you have all had a wonderful summer and are looking forward to returning to campus this fall (or perhaps in the spring if you are studying abroad).  As you already know, thanks to the generosity of SPRINT we are able to continue the NetSense study for another two years. This email contains basic information on how you can continue in the study, upgrade your phone, and what continuation will entail for you.
In short, you will be able to upgrade your phone when you arrive on campus, or for those of you studying abroad, before or after you leave the country.  In contrast to before when we had to give you phones with a special custom Android build, your new smartphones will be regular (stock) Android phones with the normal Android operating system. All in all, your phone service and general experience should be dramatically better during the next two years. 
Furthermore, the service procedure for the phones will now dramatically change allowing you to simply go to the local Sprint store to fix your phone and reinstall our research application (agent) easily on your own.  The insurance policy is also dramatically better, allowing for reduced costs on screen cracks, lost, or damaged phones. 
Upgrade Procedure
For upgrading your phone, you will have 3 upgrade choices:  

Samsung Galaxy S3 for $100.  The Galaxy S3 is Samsung’s flagship phone for 2012.
Samsung Galaxy S4 for $200.  The Galaxy S4 is Samsung’s flagship phone for 2013.
HTC One for $200.  The One is HTC’s flagship phone for 2013.

 Each of the three phone models have support for LTE (4G) and should have dramatically better WiFi and cellular reception versus the Nexus S 4G.  These are the only three phone models that are eligible for free service as part of the study. 
The fee for the phone takes care of the upgrade cost and the insurance fee (high end insurance) for the duration of the study (through May 2015).  There is no fee beyond the upgrade cost and the plan will be identical to our prior plan (i.e. free voice/text/data).  The upgrade fee is payable at the Sprint store when you upgrade your phone.
Similar to the first two years of the study, you will likely want to buy a case.  You are welcome to purchase a case in advance on Amazon or other on-line vendors.  
 For financial hardship cases, we have a limited supply of Motorola Photons and Galaxy S3’s.  Please contact netsense@nd.edu if you need to apply for financial assistance with your phone upgrade.
There are three options: Upgrade on campus when you return later this month and, for students who are studying abroad in the Fall, upgrade either prior to leaving or upon your return. No matter how you upgrade, you must send us an email at netsense@nd.edu by August 12th notifying us that you want to stay in the NetSense study and upgrade your phone.
Upgrade - On-Campus in the Fall

For those who will be on campus in the fall semester you need to tell us by August 12th via email:

That you want to be in the NetSense study another two years
Which of the above three phones you would like to have
Whether you are applying for financial assistance
You must also complete and sign a new consent form. We will be sending out this form to you within the next week.

Go to the local Sprint store located at 2031 South Bend Avenue (i.e. the Sprint store by the Martin’s at Ironwood and SR 23).  The store employees will be notified in advance that each of you are coming to upgrade and you can stop by whenever you arrive on campus. 
You must turn in your old phone to Christine Broadbent in 275 Fitzpatrick (departmental office for the Department of Electrical Engineering).
Once you have acquired your new phone, send netsense@nd.edu a note and we will send you a download link for the agent via a text message.  Similar to prior upgrades, you will simply click the link and install the software. Later in the semester, we will be upgrading the agent to a newer, more power-efficient agent.

Upgrade - Studying Abroad in Fall (before leaving)
If you are studying abroad and wish to upgrade your phone before you leave:

Let us know as soon as possible:

your mailing address
the closest location (street address) of your nearest Sprint store
the phone you would like to upgrade to. 

Once you receive a confirmation from us, please go to your local Sprint store and upgrade your phone. 
Submit your consent form electronically to netsense@nd.edu prior to leaving the country
Once you have acquired your new phone, send netsense@nd.edu a note and we will send you a download link for the agent via a text message.  Similar to prior upgrades, you will simply click the link and install the software. Later in the semester, we will be upgrading the agent to a newer, more power-efficient agent.
Return your old phone in January of 2014 when you return from studying abroad to Christine Broadbent in 275 Fitzpatrick (departmental office for the Department of Eletrical Engineering). 

Keep in mind that your phone will not work internationally and that international roaming should be disabled. You will be liable for any fees incurred while traveling internationally. It is OK to use the phone strictly over WiFi.
Upgrade - Studying Abroad in Fall (after returning)
If you are studying abroad and wish to upgrade after you return:

Send a note to netsense@nd.edu noting that you want to continue to be in the NetSense study and will be upgrading in January. Please also tell us which phone your would like.
Submit your consent form electronically to netsense@nd.edu
Upon your return in January you will be able to go to the local Sprint store to receive your new phone, and then install our agent on your new phone and return your old phone to us.

As noted above, make sure to disable international roaming with your current phone.
 Consent Form
The consent form for the study renewal will be sent in a separate email in the next week. It is quite similar to the original consent form.  As before, we are asking you to (1) use your NetSense phone as your primary communication device, and (2) complete every semester two longer surveys like you have in the past, and possibly short surveys pushed to your phone like we also did. If you do not think you can meet these two conditions, you should not re-enroll in the NetSense Study.
The main changes to the consent form are with respect to data sharing to more clearly delineate that aggregated and anonymized data may be shared with specific university and industrial partners.  Shared data is always anonymized and very carefully monitored in terms of what is shared including strict privacy controls / agreements between Notre Dame and the respective partner.
Service Procedure
Rather than having to go through the netsense@nd.edu to coordinate phone repairs, you can now simply go to the local Sprint store.  This applies whether you are on campus or are at home. 
If your repair involves acquiring a new phone, simply send us an e-mail at netsense@nd.edu and we will send you the agent link to download and install the agent once your have the new phone. 
Bringing Friends Into the Study
Starting in the second week of classes, we will invite a limited number of new people (50 or less) to join the study. You will have the opportunity to nominate any of your Notre Dame friends to join the study. If chosen to be in the study, your friends will receive a new phone (from among the three listed above) and free voice/text/data plans through May of 2015. They will also be able to port in their number from outside of Sprint (a change from when you enrolled). An e-mail will be distributed later outlining the specific details but for now, start thinking if you would like to invite any fellow students to join the study.
New Addition - Laptop Agent
We will also be requesting that you run a lightweight laptop agent in addition to the phone agent.  The laptop agent captures similar data to the phone agent and allows us to assess which sort of network activities (e.g., emailing, web surfing, Facebook updates) you do on your phone versus which activities you do on your laptop.  Further instructions for the laptop agent (which several of you are already running as part of another study) will be distributed during the first week of classes.
You will receive a $5 gift card at the end of each semester for running the laptop agent.
Please feel free to let us know if you have any questions. 
Best regards,
Profs. Striegel, Hachen, Poellabauer, Lizardo
P.S. If you have received this email in error because you have dropped out from the NetSense study, please send an email to netsenE@nd.edu immediately and let us know this.

title: NetSense Study Codebook
text:
Dear NetSense participants,
We want to thank everyone for their cooperation to date with the NetSense Study. Thank you for completing the first surveys in both the Fall and the Winter. We will shortly be releasing another round of surveys. As you will recall from the consent (or assent) form that you signed, you are required to complete these surveys in a timely manner. Because the information that you provide from these surveys is essential to our research, we need to have 100% compliance. Failure to complete the surveys will necessitate that you withdraw from the NetSense study and the free smartphone plan that you currently have will be terminated.
As you already know, there are two surveys that you need to complete each time, a demographic and attitude surveys, and a social network survey. We recommend that you set aside each time 1 hour for each survey (for a total of 2 hours).
Here is the current schedule for the remaining surveys:

Summer 2014 (which you will receive shortly)
beginning Fall semester 2014
beginning Spring semester 2015
Final Survey after Spring semester break in 2015

Again we appreciate your cooperation with this important research. If you have any questions or need additional information please do not hesitate to contact us at netsense@nd.edu
Sincerely,

The NetSense Project Team

Incentive Letter - 1/28/13
Dear NetSense Participant,
We want to thank those of you who took the time to complete these surveys by giving you a $5 Amazon gift certificate. This is not very much, but we really do appreciate the time you spent completing the surveys over the last year and half. We will be contacting you via email in the next couple weeks with the code that you can use to redeem the $5.
For those of you who have not completed the two surveys, if you do so in the next week (by Monday February 4th at 5 pm) we will also send you a $5 Amazon gift certificate.
After the current surveys, there will only be one more set of surveys at the end of this semester.
We would like to thank you again for helping us obtain the data that we need to study how social networks evolve and the effects of networks on attitudes, tastes and behaviors.
Professor David Hachen
on behalf of the NetSense Project Team
If you have any questions about the gift certificates or the surveys please do not hesitate to contact us at netsense@nd.edu or you can contact me directly at dhachen@nd.edu.

CODEBOOK
NOTES TO USERS OF THE 1971 EUROPEAN COMMUNITIES STUDY
A single codebook was created to match the data for all five countries
surveyed. The codebook was translated from the French and Belgian
questionnaires. Users who read the other languages may wish to request the
original language questionnaires in order to ascertain whether the question
wording is exactly comparable.
The data were received in OSIRIS format. The variable names appear in the
heading for each variable. In cases where the names differ, the non-conforming
names are noted next to the codes for that country. Please note that the files
are not all of the same length. In particular, several variables appear for
France that do not appear for the other countries. These variables occur at the
end of the French data file.
A card image version of the data was generated and deck and column numbers
are noted in the codebook.
The original documentation matched a pre-OSIRIS version of the data. In the
process of filebuilding codes for some variables were collapsed. The original
codes were not always updated. If the recoding of a variable was documented for
one country, the assumption was made that the same process occurred for the
other countries. This cannot be confirmed until we communicate with the
original investigator. There are also some variables for which we received no
documentation. Communication with the original investigator is necessary before
this can be recovered.

title: 1 Codebook for arcWeeklyTableCombined
text:
1 Codebook for arcWeeklyTableCombined
This codebook describes the variables in the legacy arcWeeklyTableCombined dataset.









Codebook for arcWeeklyTableCombined
…2




NetSense Study, iCeNSA, University of Notre Dame
NA


Created by Matthew J. Chandler
NA


NA
NA


General Description
NA


This dataset provides comprehensive information about mobile phone communication events from the first three years of NetSense study (August 2011 through August 2013). Additional participant-reported data on vertex and edge attributes exist in other files; this file contains only observed mobile phone communication data. The unit of observation here is an arc from sender to receiver, where both senders and receivers are either known to be or assumed to be individual persons, identified by unique numeric codes. Any reciprocal arcs (from receiver to sender) are recorded on separate rows, and there are no self-loops. Every arc has at least one study participant, which can be identified by a 5-digit ID code; all other persons have 6-digit ID codes. Most of the data for each arc are recorded in weekly increments–thus detailing the dynamics of communication over time–but the first several variables contain summary information about the arc. Week 1 begins on the official start date of the study on August 15, 2011. Week 0 captures the rare few observations before the official start date. The weekly data are censored at 107 weeks at the latest (ending September 1, 2013), but observation continued through August 2014 (binned in this dataset in week 108+). A minority of arcs are censored earlier: if the participant dropped out of the study early, then the censor date is set for 2/3 the number of total days the participant remained in the study. The censoring allows us to make judgments about whether arcs decayed before the censor date: if the last observation of communication between a sender and receiver occurred before the censor date, then that last observation is treated as the date the arc decayed, but if the last observation occurred after the censor date, then the arc is considered still effecitvely present as of the censor date. The full list of sender-receiver pairs gives the comprehensive directed network, while data from the weekly increments show the network dynamics. But please note that only mobile phone communication involving study participants is observed, so the largest complete network these data represent includes only the arcs in which both vertices are participants (easily filtered by their 5-digit ID codes).
NA


NA
NA


Variable Name
Variable Description


Sender
Unique ID code for the sender of communication (ie, the origin vertex of the arc)


Receiver
Unique ID code for the receiver of communication (ie, the terminal vertex of the arc)


FirstDate
The date of the first observation of communication, given as yyyy-mm-dd


LastDate
The date of the last observation of communication, given as yyyy-mm-dd


DurationDays
The number of days spanning from the first to the last daily observations of communication


FrequencyDays
The total number of days on which at least one communication event was observed


FirstWeekActive
The index number of the week during which the first observation of communication occurred, where week 1 begins on August 15, 2011


LastWeekActive
The index number of the week during which the last observation of communication occurred, where week 1 begins on August 15, 2011


DurationWeeksActive
The number of weeks spanning from the first to the last weekly observations of communication


FrequencyWeeksActive
The total number of weeks during which at least one communication event was observed


FirstWeekEffective
The index number of the week during which the arc is considered to have effectively formed, where week 1 begins on August 15, 2011 (equivalent to FirstWeekActive)


LastWeekEffective
The index number of the week during which the arc is considered to have effectively decayed, where week 1 begins on August 15, 2011 (right-censored; see CensorWeek)


DurationWeeksEffective
The number of weeks spanning from FirstWeekEffective to LastWeekEffective (the arc is considered effectively present for all weeks in between)


CensorWeek
The index number of the week upon which the observation of communication activity is right-censored (the maximum value possible for LastWeekEffective)


TotalFrequency_0
The total number of communication events (voice and SMS) observed before August 15, 2011


VoiceFrequency_0
The number of voice communication events observed before August 15, 2011


SMSFrequency_0
The number of SMS communication events observed before August 15, 2011


VoiceLengthSum_0
The sum of the length (in seconds) of voice communication events observed before August 15, 2011


SMSLengthSum_0
The sum of the length (in characters) of SMS communication events observed before August 15, 2011


ActiveDummy_0
A binary indicator of whether any communication events were observed before August 15, 2011


EffectiveDummy_0
A binary indicator of whether the arc is considered effectively present before August 15, 2011 (equivalent to ActiveDummy_0)


ReciprocatedDummy_0
A binary indicator of whether reciprocal communication (from receiver to sender; either voice or SMS) was observed before August 15, 2011 (“NA” if never reciprocated)


ReciprocatedWeight_0
The number of reciprocal communication events (either voice or SMS; counted in 1-to-1 pairs: sender-receiver/receiver-sender) observed before August 15, 2011 (“NA” if never reciprocated)


NonreciprocatedWeight_0
The number of unreciprocated communication events (either voice or SMS; sender-receiver only, net of reciprocal events) observed before August 15, 2011 (“NA” if never reciprocated)


WeeklyTotalFrequency_w
The total number of communication events (voice and SMS) observed during week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


CumulativeTotalFrequency_w
The cumulative total number of communication events (voice and SMS) observed up to and including week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


WeeklyVoiceFrequency_w
The number of voice communication events observed during week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


CumulativeVoiceFrequency_w
The cumulative number of voice communication events observed up to and including week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


WeeklySMSFrequency_w
The number of SMS communication events observed during week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


CumulativeSMSFrequency_w
The cumulative number of SMS communication events observed up to and including week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


WeeklyVoiceLengthSum_w
The sum of the length (in seconds) of voice communication events observed during week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


CumulativeVoiceLengthSum_w
The cumulative sum of the length (in seconds) of voice communication events observed up to and including week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


WeeklySMSLengthSum_w
The sum of the length (in characters) of SMS communication events observed during week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


CumulativeSMSLengthSum_w
The cumulative sum of the length (in characters) of SMS communication events observed up to and including week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


ActiveDummy_w
A binary indicator of whether any communication events were observed during week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


ActiveAge_w
The age of the active arc as of week w–i.e., the running count of consecutive weeks during which any communication events were observed up to and including week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


ChangeDummy_w
A binary indicator of whether ActiveDummy_w and ActiveDummy_(w-1) are different, where w ranges from 1 to 107


CumulativeChangeFrequency_w
A running count of the number of times ActiveDummy_w changed up to and including week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


EffectiveDummy_w
A binary indicator of whether the arc is considered effectively present during week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


EffectiveAge_w
The age of the effective arc as of week w–i.e., the running count of consecutive weeks during which the arc was considered effectively present up to and including week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


ReciprocatedDummy_w
A binary indicator of whether reciprocal communication (from receiver to sender; either voice or SMS) was observed during week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


ReciprocatedWeight_w
The number of reciprocal communication events (either voice or SMS; counted in 1-to-1 pairs: sender-receiver/receiver-sender) observed during week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


NonreciprocatedWeight_w
The number of unreciprocated communication events (either voice or SMS; sender-receiver only, net of reciprocal events) observed during week w, where w ranges from 1 to 107


TotalFrequency_108
The total number of communication events (voice and SMS) observed after September 1, 2013


VoiceFrequency_108
The number of voice communication events observed after September 1, 2013


SMSFrequency_108
The number of SMS communication events observed after September 1, 2013


VoiceLengthSum_108
The sum of the length (in seconds) of voice communication events observed after September 1, 2013


SMSLengthSum_108
The sum of the length (in characters) of SMS communication events observed after September 1, 2013

NoteSurvey Instructions



In this survey you will be asked questions about your personal contact network. We estimate that it will take around 30 minutes to complete this survey, though for some people it may take a bit longer.
This survey is very similar to surveys you have taken in the past, and its purpose is to obtain a description of how your social network has changed. This is important information that we will need to understand how social networks evolve during college.
All information that your provide to us through this survey is confidential. In all reports and presentations individuals will not be identifiable. Also, no one will see your answers except the researchers involved in the NetSense project.
When taking the survey you can return to previous pages by clicking the “Previous” button at the bottom of a page. Please do not use your browsers “Back” button.

1 Summer2011Net(W1)






NoteSurvey Instructions



In this survey you will be asked questions about your personal contact network. We estimate that it will take around 30 minutes to complete this survey, though for some people it may take a bit longer. You can always save your results and then return to the survey later by clicking on the link in the email we sent you.
The purpose of this survey is to obtain a baseline depiction of your social network prior to your arrival at Notre Dame. This is important information that we will need to understand how social networks change with the transition to college.

1 Fall2012Net(W4)






NoteSurvey Instructions



In this survey you will be asked questions about your personal contact network. We estimate that it will take around 30 minutes to complete this survey, though for some people it may take a bit longer.
This survey is very similar to surveys you have taken in the past, and its purpose is to obtain a description of how your social network has changed since then. This is important information that we will need to understand how social networks evolve during college.
All information that your provide to us through this survey is confidential. In all reports and presentations individuals will not be identifiable. Also, no one will see your answers except the researchers involved in the NetSense project.
When taking the survey you can return to previous pages by clicking the “Previous” button at the bottom of a page. Please do not use your browsers “Back” button.
There are 63 questions in this survey The Social Network Survey



1.0.1 Question 1: name.netid
What is your name and your NetID? Please write your answer(s) here: - [ ] First Name
Last Name

title: NetSense Study Codebook
text:
Variable Description
Raw data

btnamei: Bluetooth ID of i
btnamej: Bluetooth ID of j
episode: The order of Bluetooth detecting record for each pair of nodes within 3-minute gap
freq: number of detecting records in the episode
avg_RSSI: average RSSI of detecting records during the episode
sd_RSSI: standard deviation of RSSI of detecting records during the episode. The value is missing if there is only one records during the period
s_timestamp: The very first Bluetooth detecting time of each episode in Unix time metric
e_timestamp: The very last Bluetooth detecting time of each episode in Unix time metric
dur: The duration (in seconds) of each episode which is calculated by e_timestamp minus s_timestamp plus 60. It takes the value one if there is only one detecting record in the episode (which is identical to that the s_timestamp and e_timestamp are the same).
waitingtime: The waiting time (in seconds) between any two Bluetooth detecting episodes for each pair of nodes. The value is missing for the first record of each pair of nodes or when there is only record the pair of nodes
